title: Years Employed
statement:
Work out how many full years each employee has worked, as of July 1, 2025.

The `employees` table has `id` (integer), `name` (text), and `hired_on` (date, their first day). A year only counts once its anniversary has arrived, so someone hired on 2020-07-02 has worked 4 full years on 2025-07-01, not 5. Someone hired on 2020-07-01 has worked exactly 5.

Use the fixed date `2025-07-01`, never today's date, so the answer stays the same. Return `id`, `name`, and `years` (the number of full years) for every employee, ordered by `id`.

Expected output:

```text
 id |      name       | years
----+-----------------+-------
  1 | Priya Natarajan |    10
  2 | Marcus Webb     |     5
  3 | Elena Petrova   |     4
  4 | Tomás Herrera   |     6
  5 | Aisha Bello     |     0
(5 rows)
```
setup:
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  hired_on DATE NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO employees (id, name, hired_on) VALUES
  (1, 'Priya Natarajan', '2015-03-16'),
  (2, 'Marcus Webb', '2020-07-01'),
  (3, 'Elena Petrova', '2020-07-02'),
  (4, 'Tomás Herrera', '2018-12-31'),
  (5, 'Aisha Bello', '2024-09-10');

hints: `age(later, earlier)` returns the time between two dates as an interval in years, months, and days.
Take only the years part of that interval with `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM ...)`.

sql.starter:
-- TODO: count the full years between hired_on and 2025-07-01
SELECT id,
       name,
       0 AS years
FROM employees
ORDER BY id;
sql.solution:
SELECT id,
       name,
       EXTRACT(YEAR FROM age(DATE '2025-07-01', hired_on)) AS years
FROM employees
ORDER BY id;
